source.title: Electronic Circuit Principles of Large Language Models
source.authors: Qiguang Chen; Libo Qin; Jinhao Liu; Dengyun Peng; Jiaqi Wang; Mengkang Hu; Zhi Chen; Wanxiang Che; Ting Liu

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates whether inference-time token length predicts task accuracy, a different measurement of performance predictability from the training-scale laws in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study does not sweep model parameter count, training tokens, or training compute, or test compute-optimal training allocations. It reports a comparison between log token length and accuracy for the conventional inference-time scaling law, plus performance-prediction results using its own ECP measures. Other prompt and reasoning intervention results do not test the listed scaling-law versions.
record.test_reason: No version is tested. The study never varies model parameters, training tokens or training compute, and reports no pretraining loss. Its 'conventional inference-time scaling law' baseline correlates generated token length with task accuracy across tasks. That is a different construct from V6, which concerns downstream gains with model or training scale or with pretraining loss. The other results validate the authors' own ECP predictor or prompting strategies.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors propose a circuit analogy (Ohm's and Faraday's laws) for inference-time reasoning and in-context learning. They report that its fitted predictions correlate with accuracy better than token length (about 60% higher Pearson), and that ECP-guided strategies improve performance, including medal-level IOI and IMO 2024 results with o1-preview.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses correlations between task accuracy and inference-time token length or ECP-derived circuit quantities; it does not fit or extrapolate pretraining loss power laws.

fits_no_version.finding: Across tasks, generated token length correlates with zero-shot CoT accuracy with negative Spearman ρ (about −0.43 to −0.57) but positive Pearson r (about 0.43 to 0.54) in four LLMs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time output length predicts task accuracy across tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: ECP-predicted 'power', fitted per model, correlates with zero-shot accuracy at ρ, r > 0.7 across 9 LLMs and about 350 tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Circuit-analogy predictors built from task difficulty annotations predict LLM task accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Self-consistency and Pass@k accuracy rise with sample count with diminishing returns; the fit is improved by treating n samples as log n independent samples (Fig. 5c).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repeated-sampling accuracy scales roughly logarithmically with sample count.

record.problems: The paper's ECP validation fits some parameters using a validation set; it also reports annotation noise across nearly 350 tasks and notes relatively low R2 in those validation experiments. These limitations concern its ECP findings, not the reported negative token-length correlations.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version results left out. The paper reports numerous separate prompting, retrieval, reasoning, and downstream application results, but these do not test the listed training-scaling versions.

untested.parts: All: no loss-versus-parameters, tokens or compute sweep.
All: no fitted laws extrapolated to larger runs.
All: no other modality or training regime scaling.
All: no downstream accuracy against model or training scale or pretraining loss. Only inference-time token length and sample count are related to accuracy.
All: no fitting-choice comparison for training scaling laws.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V6 'challenges' label is dropped: token length is not scale in V6's sense, and the Spearman and Pearson signs conflict. The paper does not cite or test Kaplan- or Chinchilla-style laws.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss against parameter count, training tokens, and training compute.
Extrapolation of loss laws fitted on small training runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as training compute changes.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests inference-time generated token length as a predictor, not prediction from pretraining loss or training scale.
Dependence of training-scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and bending of training-loss curves.

rows.subject: GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared log token length with task accuracy under the conventional inference-time scaling law.

conditions.value: log token length versus task accuracy

rows.measure: Correlation between log token length and task accuracy
rows.note: The text reports the correlation range across the four models and says token length alone fails to predict reasoning performance. The reported Spearman correlations are negative.
rows.check: Generated token length per task is not model or training scale, so this row does not bear on V6. The values are also internally inconsistent: Figure 3a gives negative Spearman ρ (−0.4254 to −0.5664) but positive Pearson r (0.4262 to 0.5394). The record's 'Pearson's r < 0.53' misreads Qwen2.5-7B's r = 0.5394. 'Reversed' does not apply.

rows.subject: 9 tested LLMs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared ECP-predicted output power with observed zero-shot task accuracy.
rows.measure: Correlation between ECP-predicted power and task accuracy
rows.value: Spearman's ρ > 0.71 and Pearson's r > 0.7 across every model tested
rows.note: This is a reported aggregate for the paper's ECP-based predictor, not a test of power-law loss scaling or prediction from parameter count, training tokens, compute, or pretraining loss.
rows.check: This is the study's own ECP predictor, with per-model voltages and other parameters fitted on a validation set, compared against a baseline. It is not a claim result. The 'none' link is correct.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Four tested LLMs, with task accuracy compared against log generated-token length
reader_labels.reason: The reported Spearman correlation is negative across the tested models, and the authors state that token length alone fails to predict reasoning performance (r1).
